reason: The hypothesis relies on four key premises. The first two, concerning edge dislocation dominance and their motion in random BCC alloys, are directly supported by the cited evidence (E1 and E2). However, the third and fourth premises, which assert that coherent nanoprecipitates can be introduced into tungsten-based alloys to regulate edge dislocations and thereby enhance high-temperature properties, are not supported by the cited passages, which discuss NbTaTiV and general BCC alloys without mentioning nanoprecipitates or tungsten-based systems.
premises: Edge dislocations can be the dominant mobile dislocation type in some refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with BCC structure, unlike conventional BCC metals.
The motion of edge dislocations in a random BCC alloy is controlled by fluctuations in local solute arrangements, leading to a wavy dislocation morphology and thermally activated glide.
Coherent nanoprecipitates or nanostructural heterogeneities can be introduced into tungsten-based refractory alloys to impede and regulate edge dislocation motion.
Controlled edge dislocation motion by such obstacles enhances strain hardening and crack-tip blunting, improving high-temperature strength and toughness.
